rv.q: Beneath its somewhat overstuffedness, this is an intricately structured piece about mortality, the self and embracing second chances.
Sharp’s self-deprecation is in direct and purposeful contrast to the virtuosity of the thing he’s setting out to accomplish.
Like the most successful comedies, ta-da! makes you laugh and think — a potent combo.
There’s a lot of fun to be had watching Sharp move through the structure that he and Pinkleton have built.
Thus the sober takeaway about the significance of time, which to some degree elevates what is mostly a giddy little comedy act.
Josh Sharp’s ta-da! is an intimate reckoning with mortality, a coming-out memoir, and a parade of dirty jokes all strapped into one roller coaster of a show.
Sharp, working under Sam Pinkleton’s adept direction, is truly a magician of the solo comedy show.
I'd highly recommend spending 80 minutes with Josh Sharp. You'll leave beaming with joy.
The real triumph is his knack for storytelling, which tugs on the heartstrings as it tickles the funny bone.
Sharp draws on his immense charm and deft wit to navigate subjects that are far weightier than his upbeat title implies.

cn.t: Sharp's innovative PowerPoint-driven solo show blends comedy with weightier themes like grief and identity, earning praise for its inventive format and charm, though some find it more semi-precious than fully precious.

vr.q: All in all, would definitely recommend.
